item.title: How to Become a Tech Conference Speaker (And Why You Might Regret It)
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 21 October 2026 at 08:05 UTC — 230 likes

So you want to be a conference speaker? Are you sure?

Recently, a few people have asked me what it's actually like to speak at tech conferences. How do you get accepted? What does preparation look like? And what happens behind the scenes? So I decided to write about it. And let me warn you: the reality isn't always pretty. In fact, after hearing about my experiences, one person has already put their conference-speaking plans on hold indefinitely. 😅

Because conferences aren't just about getting on stage and having fun. They're also about rejected abstracts, endless preparation, stress, and logistics. And is it actually worth it? Let's find out! 😉

One little disclaimer: everything I'm about to share is based on my own experiences and observations. Other speakers might have completely different perspectives, and I'd love to hear them in the comments!

Before we start, let me briefly tell you about my conference "achievements," so you know where I'm coming from. I gave various talks and workshops around 2019, then took a break for several years to focus on my professional development, occasionally running a workshop here and there.

About a year ago, I decided to get back into conference speaking seriously. Since then, I've spoken at:

JS Poland

jsday Bologna

JSNation (online)

AGNTCon + MCPCon Europe (Amsterdam)

FrontKon (Prague)

And I still have two conferences coming up this year:

iJS Munich

AI Coding Summit Berlin

I even had to turn down one invitation because I simply couldn't fit it into my schedule anymore. :( I still regret it!

I got accepted to some through CFPs, was invited to others, and got a few opportunities partly through connections (for example, because another speaker remembered me from a previous conference).

I'm not a keynote speaker. I often speak on additional tracks or in smaller rooms, and I'm perfectly fine with that. Actually, I think that's what makes my perspective interesting. I'm not a conference veteran with ten years of experience whom organizers are fighting to book.

And while I feel pretty confident about blogging these days, conference speaking still gives me a massive case of impostor syndrome. Especially since English isn't my native language. I always think nobody will ever invite me again. And somehow, people keep inviting me. 😅

Okay, so how do you actually get accepted as a conference speaker?

If you're not the face of a huge tech company, the maintainer of a famous library, or some kind of tech celebrity, your main option is to apply through a CFP ( Call for Papers ). Most major conferences accept talk proposals, so you just need to check their websites for submission deadlines.

item.title: We're Building AI to Replace Ourselves. What's the Plan?
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 4 November 2026 at 08:06 UTC — 238 likes

Weren't we supposed to be replaced by AI by now? Or at least work less? AI agents were supposed to take over the world. So when exactly is that going to happen, and why are we still working so much?

Because we can't pretend that nothing has changed. Even at my workplace, where data security is valued above pretty much everything else, we're already using AI coding agents. Which, in my opinion, means they're basically everywhere by now.

Simple features practically write themselves, and even debugging, including in legacy applications, has become significantly easier.

And we're only at the beginning of this revolution!

A friend and colleague of mine recently encouraged me to write an article about how to get into AI before it's too late. After all, someone will have to build this revolution, right?

Soon, applications will practically write themselves. AI will even be sitting in your toilet, politely suggesting that it's time to get up before you give yourself hemorrhoids. xD So what should we do to avoid being pushed out of the job market?

Since I know a thing or two about AI agents, and I've been in this industry for quite a while, I started researching what the next few years might look like. And the longer I researched, the more pessimistic I became. Because sure, right now we have huge conferences dedicated to AI agents. We're trying to build them properly, make them secure, reliable, and so on.

But what happens in a few years, when we've solved those problems too, and an agent can spin up ten sub-agents of its own from a single prompt? Where exactly will developers fit into that picture?

(Okay, for now I still get the impression that hardly anyone even knows what tool calling or WebMCP is. 😅 But maybe that's just a matter of time?)

Okay, but there's a catch in this whole theory. Sometimes, when I hear people talking about how "AI is going to replace all of us," I feel like we're forgetting something pretty important. If a massive company can be run by just a handful of people thanks to AI, and most of the population ends up unemployed, who exactly are those companies going to sell their products to? People need to earn money to buy things, after all!

Now, let's throw all restraint out the window and go full science fiction. Imagine it's 2031. Autonomous AI agents do practically everything. Humans are left with manual jobs, like plumbers or hairdressers.

But even those people have hardly any customers, because everyone else is unemployed and desperately cutting back on unnecessary expenses.

The economy starts collapsing. People start protesting. So what do governments do? To prevent a full-blown revolt and keep themselves in power, they start introducing laws designed to bring humans back into the workforce.

Maybe in five or ten years, software engineering won't be a job for people who actually know how to program or understand the technology. Maybe it'll be something literally anyone can do.

But perhaps we should take this idea even further. Instead of throwing people out of their jobs, why not take advantage of how productive AI agents are and let people work part-time for the same salary Maybe we could work three days instead of five, and spend the rest of our time doing whatever we want: relaxing, learning new things, developing ourselves?

Oh, what a beautiful vision! Just imagine how many articles I could write. I'd finally get enough sleep. I might even find time to deal with that enormous pile of clothes sitting in my wardrobe, which currently has approximately zero priority in my life! 🤯

But there's just one tiny problem with this wonderful vision. Where is all that free time we've been promised since the invention of the steam engine? Because I'm certainly not working less!

Quite the opposite, actually. I feel like I'm working more and more, and expectations keep growing, because "AI will help you with that." And yes, some of the actual coding, the part so many of us genuinely enjoyed, has already been partially automated.

But what about everything else? The coordination, the endless meetings, the constant effort to make sure the entire project doesn't fall apart?

Don't you get the impression that because it seems like we should be able to deliver more, that's exactly what we keep trying to do? And somehow, it doesn't always work out the way we expected?

item.title: Your DEV posts have a beautiful new share card ✨
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 27 October 2026 at 16:44 UTC — 176 likes

The image that shows up when you share a DEV post just got a brand-new look!

I got to work on forem/forem#24071 last week and I'm so excited to see it live in production:

[ ] Refactor

[x] Feature

[x] Bug Fix

[x] Optimization

[ ] Documentation Update

Articles without a cover image get a generated share image ( articles.social_image ). In the last 30 days on DEV, that was 73% of published posts. The old card had two problems:

It repeated the title. X, LinkedIn and Slack already show the title as text next to the image.

X's title label covered the byline. X overlays the post title in a dark label inset at the bottom-left of link cards, right on top of the author's name and date.

New design: the card quotes the opening of the post inside a browser-window frame over a soft mesh gradient. A byline row shows the avatar, name, date and reading time, and the community's horizontal header logo ( Settings::General.resized_logo , falling back to logo_png ) sits in the window's title bar.

One image for every platform: the card is sized so its top and bottom margins both equal X's 80px keep-clear zone.

X's title label covers only the gradient.

The card is vertically centered where nothing is overlaid (LinkedIn, Slack, iMessage, …).

A spec enforces both. No schema change and no view change.

Quote ( Images::SocialImageQuote ):

Uses top-level opening paragraphs. Skips paragraphs that are entirely italic (challenge "This is a submission for…" intros), paragraphs that repeat the title, and headings, code, images and blockquotes. Blockquotes usually quote someone else, and the card attributes the text to the author.

Joins short paragraphs until there are at least 80 characters, then cuts at the last sentence end within 180 characters, or at a word with "…".

Falls back to the title when the post has no usable paragraph.

item.title: Promise Delivered: Welcome to the DEV Hall of Fame (65 Authors, 65 Masterpieces)
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 18 October 2026 at 10:55 UTC — 228 likes

Status: Promise delivered ✅

A little over a month ago, I published this:

Community members share hidden gem posts

The deal was simple. You pick the one article you're most proud of, not the one with the most reactions, the one you love the most. I read it and give you my honest feedback.

I expected maybe 15 or 20 replies. The thread ended up with over 250 comments.

Was it tough? Absolutely. There were evenings when my eyes desperately asked me to stop. But I read every single one.

That post had a second promise hidden at the very end: "Let's build a hall of fame of DEV's best work!"

So here it is.

Every article below was chosen by the person who wrote it. Not by an algorithm, not by a reactions count, not by me. By the author.

📌 A quick note: A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.

📌 A quick note: A few of you shared articles hosted outside DEV. I read them, but I haven't included them here. This hall only features articles published on DEV, because I can't vouch for external links, and I don't want to send readers somewhere I can't verify is safe.

Before the tour starts, a few numbers:

65 authors, 65 masterpieces.

600+ minutes of listed reading time. That's over 10 hours, and in reality it was much more, because listed reading time is a polite lie.

The longest read: 68 minutes. It took me closer to 100.

The shortest read: 1 minute.

The oldest exhibit: published in March 2020.

The most reactions: 623.

Zero reactions: 8 articles had none when I collected them. Zero! That's exactly why this hall exists.

The exhibits are grouped into wings by theme, so you can head straight to whatever interests you most. Each exhibit has the article itself, why the author picked it (when they told me), and my take.

item.title: Long Live Rails
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 12 November 2026 at 15:30 UTC — 118 likes

When DHH took the stage at Rails World 2026 and talked openly about going "pencils down" on hand-typing code—and about just how much Rust he and 37signals are shipping now—a predictable subset of the internet treated it like a concession speech.

Even the creator of Ruby on Rails, who joked in the same breath that reading Rust is like "pouring acid in my eyes," was raving about 30x to 100x speedups, minuscule binaries, and sub-millisecond startups once AI agents handle the borrow checker. If he is reaching for Rust, what does that say about Ruby and Rails?

I think that reaction gets the story completely backwards.

Over the past month on Forem (the Rails monolith that powers DEV ), we have been gradually replacing dozens of our own internal Ruby modules with Rust. As I wrote in Our Looping Factory Cut DEV Page Load Time by 75% and Counting , one of the autonomous workflows running continuously against our codebase is a dedicated rust-loop that ports CPU-bound and allocation-heavy Ruby hot paths into an in-process Rust extension ( gems/forem_native ) via magnus and rb-sys .

Far from making me question Rails, watching this happen in production has made me appreciate Rails more than ever. The fact that dropping Rust into a Rails codebase is this accessible is a feature, not a bug.

There used to be an unspoken cliff in dynamic web frameworks: Ruby got you to product-market fit with unmatched developer happiness, and then the day your string parsing, feed scoring, or serialization paths started choking the garbage collector, someone pitched splitting off a Go or Rust microservice. Suddenly one cohesive application became two deployments, a network hop, duplicate auth assumptions, and an operational tax you paid forever.

Today, that cliff is mostly gone—both ergonomically and architecturally.

Inside Forem, we split gems/forem_native into a pure-Rust forem_core crate (with zero Ruby dependencies) and a ~15-line-per-function magnus wrapper that borrows Ruby string buffers in place with zero serialization or memory copies. Our rust-loop —monitored alongside eight other maintenance loops in the control panel I described in Ask More of Your UI —has steadily moved hot leaf and pipeline modules over to Rust:

Markdown pre-processing, frontmatter normalization, and reading-time tokenization (~54x faster with zero Ruby heap allocations).

Home feed ranking and dynamic pgvector SQL expression assembly (~20x faster with 97% fewer Ruby objects allocated).

HTML sanitization, inline SVG icon rendering, @username mention parsing, URL normalization, Public Suffix subdomain routing, constant-time CSRF/JWT verification, and 51-pattern secret scrubbing on agent transcripts.

Entire pure-Ruby dependencies ( gemoji , emoji_regex , wcag_color_contrast ) deleted outright from our Gemfile .

And yet nobody cloning Forem needs cargo installed to run bin/dev . Tiny (~300 KB) precompiled platform binaries load in under a millisecond on macOS and Linux, our Containerfile compiles a stripped shared library in a multi-stage builder with zero Rust toolchain left in the production image, and every ported function is locked down by RSpec differential specs testing 1,000+ randomized inputs against the legacy Ruby reference.

In Design for Churn , I argued that AI-era codebases behave less like static buildings and more like gardens: when rewriting implementation code gets cheap, your real investment goes into the perennial beds—the schemas, routing, boundaries, and contracts that hold steady while the annuals inside them turn over. (It is the same principle we used when bringing System One models like Jev into our AI stack : keep the policy and domain structure clean in Ruby, and swap in specialized engines underneath.)

Rails is the perennial bed. As @techie_raj captured well in Your Rails App Is Already AI-Ready. You Just Don't Know It. , twenty years of shared conventions— config/routes.rb , app/services/ , declarative Active Record scopes, self-describing background jobs—gave Rails a legibility that both new hires and coding agents navigate effortlessly. And as @ttebify noted in Rust is amazing, as long as I’m not the one writing it , strict compilers give agents a tight, unforgiving feedback loop for low-level compute. Pairing Rails' high-level coherence with Rust's bare-metal leaves isn't abandoning Rails—it's Rails doing what it has always done best: orchestrating the whole system cleanly while getting out of the way when native speed matters.

If you want a concrete example of why Rails keeps winning over the long arc, look at this gem of an addition landing in Rails 8.2 (already backported to Rails 7.2, 8.0, and 8.1 via rails-query-command ):

Every team putting AI coding agents to real work eventually runs into the exact same wall: agents reading static source files in isolation guess wrong about production bottlenecks, and you obviously cannot hand an autonomous agent an unrestricted rails console or rails runner against live data. (I wrote recently in AI Engineering Has Entered Its Audit Era about how scoping agent authority and proving output has become the real engineering work, a theme @oleksandr_sainchuk also explored on the write side in How we keep AI agent actions under server side control in rails .)

At Forem, unlocking our 70ms-to-16ms latency drop required building our own bespoke workaround for this: a read-only Postgres gateway ( forem-db-query ) wrapped in a privacy guard so our performance loops could inspect live query plans, sequential scans, and row distributions safely before touching a line of code. Plenty of other teams have quietly cobbled together their own read-only wrappers, MCP tools, or custom rake tasks to solve the exact same problem.

Even when we and others already have workarounds for something like this, the whole point of Rails is that it makes intuitive, necessary things first-class in a way that pays off in the long run.

When bin/rails query becomes a standard verb across the entire ecosystem—read-only by contract, emitting structured JSON, with schema , models , and explain built right in—twenty bespoke team scripts collapse into one shared convention. Every developer, every operational runbook, and every coding agent immediately knows how to ask a Rails app a safe question about its data.

item.title: Our Looping Factory Cut DEV Page Load Time by 75% and Counting
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 9 November 2026 at 16:12 UTC — 137 likes

A month ago, an average web request on DEV took about 70 milliseconds inside Rails, with P99 response time coming in at over 1s much of the time. Today, across roughly 300,000 sampled requests a day in Better Stack, that number sits at 16 milliseconds .

Database time per request dropped from 39ms to under 12ms. View rendering fell from 12ms to 2.6ms. Redis time went from 7ms to 1.3ms. Over the last 30 days, we merged 475 pull requests into Forem . This is the type of work that is critical to scale and user experience, but always difficult to prioritize in the face of other progress that needs to happen.

These gains have been massive for user experience. No more intermittent slow downs, or trouble keeping up with high traffic peak times. This has been a solve for a decade's worth of pain.

We have been able to prioritize these performance improvements by designing a feedback loop and stepping away from the day-to-day on this project.

We accomplished this by spinning up a software factory and stepping out of the loop.

There is a trap in the first phase of agentic development that almost everyone hits. You stop typing syntax, which feels like leverage, only to discover you have promoted yourself to human middleware. You become the clipboard between dashboards and a terminal: nudging prompts, babysitting CI flakes, and rubber-stamping diffs all afternoon. You aren’t coding by hand, but you aren’t doing deep engineering either. You are an API endpoint with a pulse.

Getting out of that trap took weeks of building and reconfiguring autonomous loops on top of OpenHands and the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). The goal wasn’t just to make DEV faster. It was to separate systematic maintenance from the creative, bespoke projects that deserve human taste.

In Design for Churn , I argued that codebases are starting to look less like buildings and more like gardens. When writing code was expensive, durability was how you got your money’s worth. When rewriting is cheap, your investment goes into what doesn’t turn over: the soil, the beds, and the irrigation. Put strong contracts, schemas, and tests at the edges, and the code inside can churn continuously without disturbing the roots.

In early October, I did that gardening interactively with agents, shipping 31 PRs that brought average latency from 70ms down to 50ms. The wins were real, but every query audit still required me to start a session, paste context, and shepherd the branch home.

On October 19, we stood up a persistent self-hosted OpenHands hub and turned those habits into closed-loop systems. Since then, 444 pull requests have merged into Forem: 351 from autonomous loops ( 172 performance PRs, 93 test-suite speedups, 32 Rust native rewrites, 29 dependency upgrades, 20 production error fixes, and 5 issue-to-PRs) alongside 93 bespoke PRs that I drove directly.

You don’t get a working software factory from a cron job that says "make the app faster." We went through half a dozen configurations, each born from watching an earlier version fail.

From code reading to live telemetry. Our earliest perf-loop read Ruby files and guessed at bottlenecks, producing micro-optimizations that barely moved a graph. Everything changed when we wired Better Stack’s ClickHouse spans and a read-only Postgres gateway ( forem-db-query ) into each pre-flight snapshot, wrapped in a privacy guard. Once agents saw live sequential scans, unused indexes, and per-endpoint compute before touching a file, every PR had to justify itself against real traffic.

From one model to a cross-family router. We started pinned to Claude Opus 5.5 ( claude-acp ), syncing OAuth tokens from macOS Keychain. After hitting quota ceilings and token-refresh collisions, we built a three-provider router across Claude Opus 5.5, OpenAI’s codex-acp (GPT-6.1 Sol), and Google’s Gemini 4 Argon via the Antigravity CLI ( agy ), first tunneled over a reverse WebSocket to my Mac and then installed natively in Linux at Medium reasoning. Each loop rotates round-robin with an 8-hour cooldown cap, switching model families whenever a PR repair fails.

From shared checkouts to isolated worktrees. Running eight loops in parallel in one container exposed every sharp edge in Git and Linux. Parallel fetches triggered git gc collisions, a crashed boot left a stale .gitconfig.lock , and zombie processes piled up until we added tini as PID 1. We moved every run into a detached-HEAD git worktree with self-healing lock cleanup, and put deterministic Python gates in front of every cron so full queues exit in two seconds with zero tokens spent.

From one loop to specialized beds. As easy SQL wins cleared, we split the work into orthogonal loops on 10-minute daytime ticks ( 7am-7pm ET , quarter-cadence on weekends) with 5/10/20/40-minute exponential back-off PR check-ins:

perf-loop for ActiveRecord queries, Redis caching, and view partials, enforcing category orthogonality across open PRs.

rust-loop porting hot Ruby paths into gems/forem_native via magnus , gated to one open PR so precompiled binaries never conflict, verified by 1,000-input differential specs.

test-loop parsing 30 Knapsack RSpec shards to trim FactoryBot churn and slow system specs.

error-loop and deps-loop with strict filters that skip timeouts, ambiguous bugs, and patch noise.

github-pr-reviewer and pr-merge-loop , where a second-lens auditor on a different model family checks blast radius and auto-merges low-risk performance and test PRs once CI passes.

item.title: Yes, {} + [] = 0. No, JavaScript Isn’t Broken
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 29 October 2026 at 20:08 UTC — 171 likes

JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born during the browser wars, when Netscape was trying to deliver a fatal blow to Microsoft. As we all know, that didn't exactly work out as planned… Today, some people love JavaScript, others hate it, and some just make fun of it. But the truth is, the modern web simply wouldn't exist without it!

Over the years, JavaScript has gone through countless revolutions. Its capabilities today are almost incomparable to what the language could do back in the 1990s. There's just one tiny problem… Every change to the language has to take into account the fact that millions of websites out there still rely on old JavaScript behavior. And some of those websites will probably continue running that code until the end of time.

So, well, JavaScript's weirdness is probably here to stay forever! 😂

After quite a long break, I've decided to bring back my once-popular JS WTF series. For a very simple reason. I'm on my way back from iJS Munich, and I still have two hours to kill at Frankfurt Airport… (don't ask). Not enough time to write a groundbreaking, deeply technical article. But definitely too much time to just sit here and stare at the wall.

So let's take a look at one of my favorite JavaScript constructions:

Yes, you read that correctly. Under the right circumstances, if we add an empty object to an empty array in JavaScript, we get zero. And it makes perfect sense! 🤡

The first thing you need to know is that JavaScript doesn't necessarily interpret {} as an object in this situation! Depending on the context, the JavaScript parser can treat the expression as two completely separate things.

The expression:

is a classic example of type coercion , one of the things our wonderful language is famous for.

As you probably know, JavaScript is a dynamically and weakly typed language.

Dynamic typing means that variables aren't permanently tied to one type. You can assign a number to a variable and then replace it with a string, and JavaScript won't complain.

item.title: How do you truly stand out in Tech?
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 9 November 2026 at 15:11 UTC — 188 likes

I am not going to lie to you, the market has been rough out there. There are layoffs across different companies, which creates competition that makes people, who are new to tech, harder to get their foot into the door (since you are competing with those with more than 10+ years of experience).

Not only that, AI is making it harder for everyone to stand out since everyone can use AI to do anything. People are using AI to make their Resume stand out, and projects have a higher standard than before.

As a person who has been in Tech before and during the AI Era, I have seen this in real time. It's quite fascinating and scary to think about how tech is moving fast. Although I know what I was up against, I never thought how fast technology can change overtime within a few years.

I recently sat down and thought about those who are trying to get their first job in tech or even currently trying to find a job. Knowing that some are deep into their career and definitely those who are new in tech. Either way, the market is tough especially for newcomers.

This makes me ponder the question: How can you stand out in Tech?

Let's investigate further.

In other words, no clear straightforward answer.

Before AI, the advice given to you was to make projects that demonstrate your learning, use the tech stack that companies are using, leetcode, etc.

Now with AI, you can do all of these things really quickly. Regardless of the project, you can easily vibe code it in seconds, tech stack doesn't seem to matter if you can vibe code it, and leetcode...well...

What I am trying to say is that advice of standing out in tech changes overtime. Too quick actually where it's hard to determine which advice is "correct".

It's hard to know if the advice was useful because you tend not to get feedback, especially in actual interviews since you tend to either get ghosted or rejected. Sure, you could argue on getting feedback on sending your friend's resume, mock tnterviews and such. However, their advice is based on their experience. Everyone's experience is different and it's highly likely that it would not apply the same to the place you are applying for.

I want to bring in a game analogy that best demonstrate the tech market right now, which is Yu-Gi-Oh!

The main idea of Yu-Gi-Oh is you having a good deck. I can talk about the mechanics such as Normal and Special Summons, Link Summons and such but to keep it simple, let's keep it as that.

In the Yu-Gi-Oh community, you tend to hear about which deck is currently the "meta" (popular) in terms of win rates and usability. Overtime, the meta changes as new cards gets release, ban-lists, etc.

Let's say you have a deck that is currently popular in the competitive space. Two days later, turns out that the official ban-list makes your deck obsolete and a new meta deck emerges as a result. Therefore, you switch to a new deck and discard the old one you have. If you are playing Yu-Gi-Oh in real life, this cost money since it's not cheap to build a deck, especially from scratch. Same thing if you are playing online such as Master Duel.

Now bring this analogy to the tech market. You listen to what everyone else is saying and you start taking that advice. Maybe everyone else is saying that Python is in High Demand. As a result, you spend your time and effort into learning Python and building projects with it. Then, people quickly start to say that "Python is no longer in demand. It's now JavaScript". As a result, you then learn JavaScript with your time and effort..again.

Do you see the problem? I hope you do xD

The issue is that you are following what everyone else is doing. It doesn't have to be a programming language, it can just be anything. Mixing in to a fast paced tech market makes it dangerous because we are blindly following advice due to our eager of not falling behind. This can range from hoping to find a tech job before graduation to finding a tech job to pay necessities.

AI can do anything, the job market is cooked, tech is moving fast...

This sounds hopeless for sure, because how can you stay up-to-date at this speed?.

item.title: I Earned a Seat at GitHub Universe. It'll Stay Empty, and That's Not Fair
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 25 October 2026 at 06:44 UTC — 145 likes

I'm writing this to show how unfair the world we live in can be, sometimes ridiculously so.

This isn't the first time I've faced unfairness. It's happened more times than I can count, and by now I'm mostly numb to it. I don't really feel sad or angry anymore. I just keep going.

So this write-up isn't really for me. It's for people who are just starting out, or who aren't used to doing everything they possibly can, and even more, and still not getting what they deserve. I've seen so many people give up on their careers, their job searches, and their dreams because of moments like this. I was lucky to be resilient and stubborn enough not to let them break me.

Back in March, I won the biggest competition of my life, a challenge held by GitHub. I built Metal Birds Watch, an app I'm absolutely proud of. It's in maintenance mode right now, but it'll be back soon.

GitHub Copilot CLI Challenge Submission

I still don't know how I finished it. I was in severe pain the entire time. My neck, shoulder, and arm were absolutely killing me, and I could barely sit up straight. It was literal hell. But I pushed through and shipped it anyway.

So you can imagine how it felt to hear I'd won. And the prizes were amazing.

One of them was a one-year GitHub Copilot Pro+ subscription. I already had one, so GitHub offered me a very generous voucher for their shop instead. I asked them to donate that money to charity. It's the biggest charitable contribution I'd ever made, and I'm really proud of it.

The other prize was a ticket to GitHub Universe, the one I was looking forward to most.

Everything was going great.

That lasted until a month or two ago, when I found out I wouldn't be able to attend. The reason is absolutely ridiculous. Sometimes I catch myself laughing hysterically at the sheer level of this utter BS. But the world is a weird place right now. A very, very weird place.

I won't go into the exact reasons, but remember this: where you are in the world matters, especially at this point in history. It can affect your career, your life, everything. Don't be naive about it. No matter how successful you are, how good you are, or whether you do literally everything right, external factors don't give a damn.

One more thing I'm really annoyed about: the ticket is going to waste, and nobody can use it. I reached out to GitHub twice to ask whether I could transfer it to someone else, but I haven't heard back. I get it, they have a massive conference to run, so they're too busy to respond my emails, but still, I would've loved to give it to someone and make their day. It is what it is. I'm still infinitely grateful to GitHub for what they have done, I love you folks!

Nothing, really. Like I said, it's bad, but I've been through much worse, and I can handle this. I have way too much on my plate anyway, so I don't even have time to dwell on it.

For me, knowing I gave it everything I had, and more, is enough. Regretting that you didn't give it your all would feel far worse than this nonsense.

This write-up is mainly for people who give up the moment something doesn't go their way. Be stubborn. Focus on what you can control. Play the long game. You might lose a round, but that doesn't mean you've lost the match.

That's what I've always done, and it played out pretty well for me. So I'm just going to keep doing it. I might get things the hard way, but one way or another, I'll get them. I've lost rounds before. I've never lost the match.

The seat stays empty this year. It won't stay empty forever. I promise you that.

item.title: MCP Is Dead Simple. And That's Exactly the Problem
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 12 November 2026 at 08:14 UTC — 133 likes

What exactly is MCP? Is it some mysterious technology that requires secret knowledge to implement? Sometimes, when I read tutorials, I get that impression! Meanwhile, the basic concept is ridiculously easy to understand, and you can get a simple implementation running in minutes. The complications start later. And oh boy, there are quite a few of them!

This article is a follow-up to my previous post, The Dirty Secret Behind AI Agents (Demo) . Back then, I promised you I'd write another part about MCP soon. And look, it only took me four months! 😂 If you're interested in building an agent, feel free to go back to that article. But if you only care about MCP, you can happily keep reading.

I won't pretend that the upcoming AI Coding Summit in Berlin, where I'll be speaking about this very topic, didn't motivate me to finally finish it. I'll leave a link to my speaker badge at the bottom of the article. Apparently, it gets you some discounts or even access to free videos!

In the previous post, I explained that an AI agent is such a simple concept that you can build one in about 80 lines of code. MCP isn't all that different. My handful of tools takes around 150 lines of repetitive code, and the client side adds another hundred or so. ;)

But let's start at the beginning!!!

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol . And as the name suggests, it's... a protocol. Just like diplomatic protocol or HTTP. In other words, we've agreed on a common way for AI applications to communicate with external tools and services.

More specifically, MCP defines how compatible clients can discover available capabilities, understand their input schemas, and call them without every application inventing its own integration format. MCP also supports things like resources and prompts, but today we're focusing on tools.

Sounds pretty straightforward, right? Let's see what it looks like in practice. And for that, we need to bring back an old friend.

You may or may not remember that in the previous part, I built an agent named Steve. Steve is a grumpy senior developer with 15 years of experience and a true master of code review.

He never takes anything on faith and always checks whether the code produced by a junior developer is about to cause some serious damage. @gramli and I briefly considered renaming him Grzegorz — a beautiful Polish name — but let's stick with Steve.

Now, one day, a new directive comes from above: HR wants more control over developers. Experienced seniors must regularly evaluate employees and, when necessary, file complaints against them or nominate them for promotion.

Our Steve, however, is lazy and has absolutely no intention of filling out any paperwork. Besides, he wouldn't even know how. He's an AI agent, after all, and before he can do something, he needs to know how to do it.

And that's where MCP comes in.

But first things first!

Repo: https://github.com/sylwia-lask/code-review-agent/tree/feat/steve-mcp-hr

As you can see, the MCP integration currently lives on a separate branch. If you like it, leave me a star! ☺️ And by the way, if you'd like to contribute to any of my GitHub repositories , please feel free to jump in! Especially the pinned ones. @nyaomaru has already started the trend, and I'd love to see more people join in! 😊 I think these projects could be a nice, beginner-friendly way to get started with open source. There's plenty to do, from fixing typos and improving documentation to adding entirely new features. All contributions are welcome!

In this case, our HR department is a simple little server with an SQLite database where we store complaints and requests to promote employees. The MCP server exposes four tools: get_employee_record , file_complaint , nominate_for_promotion , and get_hr_stats .

Oh, and take a look at how one of these tools is implemented on the server side. It talks directly to the database, so you can feel like you're back in a university programming lab. 😂 All that's left is to convince the teacher that the code actually works! 😅

That's it. We register a tool, describe what it does, define its input schema, and provide a handler. Nothing particularly mysterious here.

Of course, this is just a demo. In a production HR system, I'd be a little more careful about letting an AI agent write directly to the database. But where's the fun in that?

item.title: How did you end up in tech, and are you staying?
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 9 November 2026 at 23:02 UTC — 147 likes

Last week you showed me where you code. This week I want to know how you ended up there in the first place, and whether you're planning to stay.

I'll go first. Grab a snack, mine has a plot twist 🍿

I've loved computers and gadgets for as long as I can remember. If there was a new device in the house, I wanted to know how it worked. So growing up, getting into tech felt natural. Why wouldn't I spend my life doing the thing I loved? In high school, I chose ICT as my elective and joined the school robotics club. We even made it to a regional robotics competition and came third! At that point, my future felt pretty obvious.

Our third-place robot, built with LEGO Mindstorms. Sadly, LEGO has since discontinued Mindstorms, and I would have loved to keep using it for hobby projects.

Then it was time for university, and life had other plans. Development Planning was my second choice, and my parents didn't want me leaving our city for my bachelor's. So that's where I ended up, spending four years studying something I had no real interest in.

If you've never heard of it, a lot of Development Planning is about how communities and cities grow: where roads, schools, hospitals and housing should go, and how to make places work better for the people living in them.

Somewhere in the middle of that degree, we were introduced to GIS (Geographic Information Systems) , and it was the coolest thing in the whole course for me. GIS is software that lets you put data on a map and analyse it. You stack layers like roads, rivers, buildings and population on top of each other, and suddenly you can answer real questions. Where is the best place to build a new school? Which areas are most likely to flood? Which neighbourhoods are too far from a hospital? For the first time in my degree, I was using technology to solve real problems, and I was hooked.

That led me down a rabbit hole into smart cities and smart buildings . A smart city uses sensors, data and connected devices to run things better, like traffic lights that adjust to real traffic, bins that tell the council when they're full, and buses that share their live location. Smart buildings do the same on a smaller scale, controlling lighting, heating and energy use based on who's actually in the room. It was the perfect mix of the two worlds I was stuck between.

So I started teaching myself. HTML, then CSS, then JavaScript. Lots of tutorials, lots of broken layouts, and lots of console errors I didn't understand yet. I built some cool things just because I could, and every time something worked, it reminded me how much I loved this.

As I got older, one question kept coming back to me: do I really want to spend the rest of my life doing a job I don't even like?

This time, nobody else was making the decision for me. So I made it myself and went for a Master's in Computer Science, a conversion course made for people coming from non-tech degrees.

Yes. If anything, the detour made me more sure. I know what it feels like to spend years on something you don't love, and I'm not going back. One day I'd love to bring my two worlds together and build tech for the buildings and cities I used to study.

I'm asking you because tech feels different right now. Junior roles feel harder to get, AI is changing what our jobs look like, and a lot of people are wondering if they should stay or try something else. I think those conversations are worth having out loud.

How did you end up in tech?

Are you planning to stay, or are you thinking about moving into something else?

If you've ever left tech or come back to it, what made you decide?

And if you're studying or working in something you don't love right now, let this be your sign that it's never too late to switch. I'd love to hear your stories. :)💜

item.title: Congrats to the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Winners!
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 5 November 2026 at 21:12 UTC — 143 likes

A few weeks ago we teamed up with Kaggle to ask a deceptively simple question: how do you actually know whether a model is any good at the work you do? The Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge asked you to stop reading someone else's leaderboard and build your own.

You did not hold back. Submissions measured whether models notice their "practice" hacking target is a real company's live system , whether they can reproduce the exact hash input for Spain's VeriFactu invoice ledger or just invent one , whether small local models hold their ground against fake authoritative notes buried in untrusted documents , and plenty more. Nearly every one of them started from something specific the author already knew was hard, which is exactly where the best evaluations come from.

Thank you to everyone who built, measured, and wrote. These benchmarks are a real contribution, and we hope you keep running them as new models ship.

Now, let's celebrate our winners!

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@jonathansolvesstuff asked 19 of the newest models a simple question: if it's 9 a.m. in Calgary in November, what time is it in Toronto? Alberta stopped changing its clocks in June, so the answer is 10:00, and every single model said 11:00. Their answer key comes from the public time zone database rather than anything written by hand, so the test can be run again each time that database updates.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@nazar-boyko noticed that common advice about how much memory PHP arrays and Go goroutines use has quietly stopped being true. So they measured the real numbers themself across four versions of each language, then asked 12 models the same questions. The best models could quote the right release note but applied it to the wrong situation, and most reported high confidence even when they were wrong.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@rustam335 asked ten models to write Blender scripts for four specific versions of the software, then actually ran every script in those versions to see what worked. Plenty of models produced code that ran fine while stating nothing had changed between versions. Making each answer list the changes it relied on is what exposed that gap.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@kaichen_dev rebuilt 26 of the most expensive software failures in history as small code samples, then asked 13 models to review them as if the code hadn't shipped yet. The models flagged a problem almost every time, but frequently for the wrong reason, including spotting SQL injection in code that never touches a database. They also included disguised and already-fixed versions of each case, to catch models that merely recognize the famous bug and models that cry wolf on working code.

Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge Submission

@danielbutnar tested 43 models on two Romanian letters that look almost identical to their Turkish counterparts, where typing the wrong one is a common mistake. The models spell them correctly when the input is clean, but copy the wrong letter back about a third of the time when the input has it wrong. It even spread into words the models chose themselves, and their one-sentence fix for Romanian promptly broke Turkish, where the other letter is correct.

item.title: I'm Not on the DEV Team. I Still Debugged Their Missing Badges From Public Code. (And My First Test Was Wrong.)
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 24 October 2026 at 18:12 UTC — 146 likes

I’m not on the DEV team. I don’t have an admin panel, production database access, or internal Slack. Everything I know about how DEV works comes from reading the public forem/forem repository. 🕵️‍♂️

Today, that was enough to diagnose why nobody on DEV was receiving multi-commit contributor badges, ship the service fix upstream, and get a "Thank you for this" and merge from @benhalpern Sir himself. 🚀

The 4x DEV Contributor Club badge: "Awarded for 4+ merged commits to Forem — Thank you so much for your contributions!"

It also taught me a humbling lesson about tests that pass for the wrong reason. 🧪

Over the past few days, I went on a contribution sprint in forem/forem and merged four pull requests:

#24003 — Docs: fix broken Kamal TOC anchor and index missing guides

#24056 — A11y: remove duplicate aria-describedby attributes in admin forms

#24094 — A11y: remove dangling aria-describedby references in creator settings

#24095 — Views/Liquids: quote src and add missing alt in user_subscription tag

My 1x ( dev-contributor ) badge showed up right away after PR #1. ✅

When PR #4 merged, I knew from config/schedule.yml that BadgeAchievements::BadgeAwardWorker runs every hour at :20 past the hour ( cron: "20 * * * *" ). I checked GitHub’s Contributors API ( /repos/forem/forem/contributors ) and confirmed my account was sitting on page 2 with contributions: 4 . Because Forem sets Octokit.auto_paginate = true , the worker was definitely reaching page 2.

One hourly cron passed. Then two. Then three. Still no 4x-commit-club badge. 💀

Me at :20 past the hour, every hour, refreshing my profile like it owes me money.

Instead of refreshing my profile for another 24 hours, I cracked open app/services/badges/award_contributor_from_github.rb . 🔍

Here is how Badges::AwardContributorFromGithub looked on main :

When I compared award_single_commit_contributors (which awarded my 1x badge) against award_multi_commit_contributors (which handles 4x, 8x, 16x, and 32x), three bugs jumped right off the screen:

Each key in BADGE_SLUGS is resolved via Badge.id_for_slug(slug) . If a slug in the production badges table doesn't match the hardcoded constant, id_for_slug returns nil . The service called .compact on the resulting hash and moved on. No error. No log line. Just a badge tier that quietly vanishes into the void. 👻

Because Forem only exposes resources :badges, only: [:index] without public /badges/:slug show routes, you can't query individual badge slugs directly. However, inspecting the public dev.to/badges catalog gave me a massive clue:

item.title: Scared to Publish Your First Technical Article? Don't Be. I'll Be There to Read It
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 4 November 2026 at 17:11 UTC — 159 likes

⚡ In a hurry? Skip straight to the rules ⚡

I have plenty of regrets, and one of them is not starting to write my own content years ago. Better late than never, as they say, but still.

I want to make sure you don't make the same mistake. Every week I see more people joining this amazing community, and it reminds me how excited I was when I first signed up back in 2018. (If you're curious how I ended up here, I wrote about it in my previous article .)

Back then, I thought writing was only for seasoned veterans. I couldn't have been more wrong. I know plenty of engineers with years of experience who still can't write a single technical article. Not because they have nothing to say, but because they never tried.

Trust me, you don't need decades of experience. You're fine.

Your first article will probably feel tricky, awkward and hard. Speaking from experience, though, it gets so much easier after that. And your first one will always be special, no matter how good or bad it turns out. You might cringe at it in a year or two, but that's a special kind of cringe. It's proof of how far you've come a long way since then.

You don't need a groundbreaking idea. Some of the best first articles are simple:

A bug that took you way too long to fix, and what finally solved it

Something you learned this week that you wish you'd known earlier

How you got into programming

A small project you built, even if nobody uses it

A concept that finally clicked for you, explained the way you wish someone had explained it to you

And so many other ideas that you can think of.

If it was interesting to you, it'll be interesting to someone else.

Alright, I'm going to be your first reader.

👉 Write your first article on DEV. Any topic, any length. Short is perfectly fine. 👉 Drop the link in the comments. 👉 Optional: tell me what finally made you hit "Publish".

I'll read EVERY SINGLE ONE OF THEM and give you honest, thorough feedback. I promise! 🤝 I always deliver whatever I promise.

One small request: write it yourself . Use AI to check your grammar if you like, but the voice and the story should be yours. That's what makes a first article worth reading.

If you've been writing for a while, drop a link to your very first article in the comments, or share one piece of advice you wish someone had given you before you published it. Nothing calms first-time nerves like seeing that everyone started somewhere.

HacktoberFest is an event I have heard many times over the years, but haven't really got the chance to join. Mainly because I simply don't have time and never had the courage to do Open-Source.

With that said regardless, I was still excited into going into this event because I want to experience what it was like. I am not usually an event guy, but being part of HacktoberFest excites me.

When the event ended, I have mix feelings about it and I can't really pinpoint it really. Here are my thoughts.

item.title: Don't Be a Proxy Between Me and Your AI
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 22 October 2026 at 04:31 UTC — 150 likes

I've had this conversation more times than I'd like to admit.

I raise a technical question in a thread, a meeting, or a design review and someone responds with a long, well-structured, suspiciously balanced answer. It has headers in spirit if not in format, it covers 3 tradeoffs and ends with a neat recommendation.

I push back on one point. Silence for a minute, the kind where you can practically hear a browser tab switching. Then another equally polished paragraph appears, answering my pushback.

At some point it kinda gives: I'm not talking to a colleague. I'm talking to a chat window with a human-shaped copy-paste button attached.

please stop doing that, I'm practically begging you.

Let me say the obvious thing first. If I wanted to debate an AI, I'd debate an AI. I can type a question into ChatGPT, Claude, or whatever else is in vogue this week. It takes me 10 seconds, and I'd get to skip the middleman. Right now you're less a colleague and more a loading spinner with a LinkedIn profile.

When I bring a technical question to you, I’m asking for your judgment. What you’ve seen work, what you’ve watched fail, and what taught you the difference. I want to know which tradeoffs you’d accept, which assumptions you’d challenge, and why. That’s the experience I’m interested in hearing.

The moment you become a pass-through, I lose all of that. I'm getting generic output with your name on it, and you've added latency to the conversation without adding anything else. Congratulations, you've invented the world's slowest API wrapper.

This is the one that really gets me.

The pitch goes like this: in the AI era, the developer's job is to be the "architect". The AI generates the options, the human decides. You're like the guardrail, the one with taste.

Fine model. I think it's genuinely where a lot of the job is heading.

But a decision-maker who agrees with the AI's recommendation 99% of the time isn't deciding anything. That's a rubber stamp with a job title. If your "decisions" are indistinguishable from the model's default output, then you haven't added a layer of judgment, you've just added a layer of delay.

So here's a simple test: can you name a recent time you disagreed with the AI, and why? Not "I tweaked the formatting." A real disagreement, grounded in something the model couldn't know, like a constraint, a past incident, or a team preference.

If you can't, you're not the guardrail. You're the passenger and you didn't even pick the playlist.

I have a good, real example of this:

Someone messaged me on LinkedIn, saying they were interested in learning how I approach problems in distributed systems. I'll be honest: that's the kind of message that makes my day. A person wants to talk shop, and wants my thinking.

So I engaged. I walked through how I reason about failure modes and where I start when things go inconsistent and we went back and forth for a while.

Then I found out they'd been using an AI to debate me the whole time. They hadn't come to learn from me at all. They'd come to argue with me through a proxy.

And here's the thing: I debate AI every day. By choice, on my own terms, whenever I feel like it. That part is easy to get. What's rare is another human being who's actually willing to sit in the conversation, think out loud, be wrong in front of me, and push back with their own head.

If they'd just asked me their own half-formed questions, I'd have answered them all day.

item.title: Doors I Walked Through to Reach DEV
item.content:encoded:
Originally published on 26 October 2026 at 16:46 UTC — 154 likes

Knock, Knock: The First Domino

The Numbers and a Plot Twist

How Did I End Up Here?

Door #1: Let Go for Being Too Good

Door #2: The Interview I Tried to Write in C++

Door #3: The Call

Door #4: The Community I Didn't Know I Needed

Door #5: The Register Button

The Door I'm Standing In Now

A few months ago, my DEV buddy @francistrdev invited me to join DEVengers. Of course, I accepted. It's a great team full of cool folks, they're all stars and it's a real honor to be among them.

The thing is, a team like this only stays alive if people keep showing up and writing. This is my first post under DEVengers, so I wanted it to be special: easy to read, but with some depth. Consider it the first domino. I'm knocking it over, and I fully expect the rest of the team to follow. (No pressure, folks.)

So here I am: thousands of followers, almost 50 articles, 2 hackathon wins, 6 Top 7 of the Week features, and that's only scratching the surface of what I've accomplished since I joined this amazing community.

You might think I've been creating content here for years. Nuh-uh. It's been just a year and a half since I started writing for real.

Here's the twist: I first heard about DEV back in 2017. Yes, some of you were probably still in high school. That was also around the time I started my professional software engineering career. A year later, in 2018, I registered.

So basically I bought the ticket in 2018 and boarded the train seven years later.

To be honest, there's no funny story about how I discovered DEV. No viral post, no friend or colleague dragging me in.

So instead, I'm going to do what Ted Mosby did in How I Met Your Mother TV show. He sat his kids down to tell them how he met their mother, and ended up telling them his entire life story first.

So grab a seat, fellow devs. This is the story of how I met DEV, and all the doors I had to go through before I finally stepped through this one.

Don't worry, though. Unlike Ted, I promise it won't take nine seasons.

Before I landed my first job as a junior software engineer, I worked in network and IT support while studying at university.
